name: Graph Autoencoder Benchmark (GAE Benchmark)
description: Graph autoencoders (GAEs) are self-supervised learning models that can learn meaningful representations of graph-structured data by reconstructing the input graph from a low-dimensional latent space. Over the past few years, GAEs have gained significant attention in academia and industry. In particular, the recent advent of GAEs with masked autoencoding schemes marks a significant advancement in graph self-supervised learning research. While numerous GAEs have been proposed, the underlying mechanisms of GAEs are not well understood, and a comprehensive benchmark for GAEs is still lacking. In this work, we bridge the gap between GAEs and contrastive learning by establishing conceptual and methodological connections. We revisit the GAEs studied in previous works and demonstrate how contrastive learning principles can be applied to GAEs. Motivated by these insights, we introduce lrGAE (left-right GAE), a general and powerful GAE framework that leverages contrastive learning principles to learn meaningful representations. Our proposed lrGAE not only facilitates a deeper understanding of GAEs but also sets a new benchmark for GAEs across diverse graph-based learning tasks. The source code for lrGAE, including the baselines and all the code for reproducing the results, is publicly available at https://github.com/EdisonLeeeee/lrGAE.
evaluation_method: task-specific metrics: AUC / Average Precision (AP) for link prediction, classification accuracy/F1 for node classification, reconstruction error for graph reconstruction
general_score_metric: AUC / AP for link prediction and accuracy/F1 for node classification
typical_sota_score: varies widely by dataset and task; not reported as a single unified percentage
reputation: Newly proposed benchmark framed around GAEs and contrastive principles; limited adoption so far but relevant to graph representation learning researchers.
notes: Non-LLM benchmark; heterogeneous graph datasets and task protocols can make cross-model comparisons difficult; code released for reproducibility, but results depend on masking strategy, augmentation, and graph preprocessing choices.
